Aaron Burr was the third Vice President of the United States under Thomas Jefferson, serving from eighteen hundred one to eighteen hundred five. He remains one of the most controversial and enigmatic figures of the founding era. During his vice presidency, Burr was isolated from power and sidelined by the president's Republican faction. The defining moment of his life came in eighteen hundred four when he shot and killed Alexander Hamilton in a dawn duel in Weehawken, New Jersey over insults related to Hamilton's opposition to Burr's political ambitions. This duel destroyed Burr's political career entirely. He ran for the New York gubernatorial office and the U.S. Senate, but his ambitions collapsed in the scandal that followed. After his vice presidency, Burr attempted to establish an independent empire in the western frontier, allegedly scheming to separate territories from the United States and place himself at the head of a new nation. He was tried for treason in eighteen hundred seven for his alleged conspiracy to invade Spanish territory and establish a western republic, but was acquitted. After his acquittal, Burr fled to Europe to escape creditors and political enemies, spending years in exile before returning to America to practice law. His complex legacy remains defined by the Hamilton duel and the western schemes that shaped the geopolitics of early American expansion.
